entries.title: Magic UI
entries.prompt:
# Use Magic UI in a project

Source: Magic UI, https://magicui.design, MIT. Pinned upstream commit `efe76fc5755eca1142dd4f74c1d6f0ace2887e3c`.
Rights: permissive. Install components from upstream and keep the MIT notice.

## Goal

Add one or two animated marketing components to an existing shadcn/ui project without turning the page into a demo reel.

## Use it when

- The page already has shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS variables.
- One section needs a marquee, a text effect, a beam, a globe or a small interaction.
- The team accepts the motion dependency that some components bring.

## Build steps

1. Confirm the project has shadcn/ui initialized and a working Tailwind theme.
2. Pick a component from the vault entry or the component index at `sources/magic-ui/components.md`.
3. Read the component page for its dependencies. Several use Motion or a canvas library.
4. Install one component at a time:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/marquee
   npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/number-ticker
   ```

5. Review the generated file as your own code. Change the defaults, remove unused props, and match the project tokens.
6. Add reduced-motion handling for any continuous animation. The registry does not always include it.
7. Keep the MIT notice in the project. Magic UI is MIT, and the components are copied into your source tree.

## Requirements

- Install only what the page uses. Do not bulk-add the registry.
- Check the bundle impact of canvas and motion dependencies.
- Every component keeps a visible focus state and a reduced-motion path.
- Text effects stay off controls and body copy.
- Components match the project palette instead of shipping the demo colors.

## Do not

- Do not copy the whole registry into the project.
- Do not use the components as the only copy of meaningful content.
- Do not remove the MIT notice.
- Do not present Magic UI components as original work.

## Verify

- `npm run build` passes with no unused dependency warnings.
- Reduced motion stops continuous animations.
- The new section works at 320px and 1440px.
- The license notice is present.

## Attribution

Magic UI, MIT, https://magicui.design. Keep the MIT notice when copying components.
entries.summary: Animated components built on top of shadcn/ui, aimed at marketing pages and landing experiences. Installed from the `@magicui` registry with the shadcn CLI.

entries.title: React Bits
entries.prompt:
# Use React Bits in a project

Source: React Bits by David Haz, https://reactbits.dev, MIT plus the Commons Clause. Pinned upstream commit `e12c22192ac7b4b452c5e2feb9b586d74765d696`.
Rights: restricted. **Do not copy or redistribute the components.** Install them from upstream into the target application only.

## Goal

Use one React Bits component inside an application or product, including a commercial one, without violating the Commons Clause.

## Use it when

- A specific component, such as SplitText, BlurText or a background effect, fits the design.
- The component will live inside your application and will not be sold, sublicensed or redistributed as a component.
- The project can carry the component's dependencies.

## Build steps

1. Choose the language and styling suffix: `JS` or `TS`, then `CSS` or `TW`. For example, `SplitText-TS-TW`.
2. Install from upstream into the target project:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add @react-bits/SplitText-TS-TW
   ```

   Or:

   ```bash
   npx jsrepo@latest add https://reactbits.dev/r/SplitText-TS-TW
   ```

3. Read the generated file and its dependencies before using it.
4. Adapt it to the project tokens and remove unused options.
5. Keep the React Bits license notice and attribution in the project.
6. Add reduced-motion handling if the component animates continuously.

## Requirements

- The component is used inside an application, website or product.
- The application is not primarily a component library, template marketplace or port collection.
- The component is not resold, sublicensed, bundled as a component pack or republished as a port.
- Accessibility basics are checked: focus, labels, reduced motion, keyboard access.

## Do not

- Do not copy React Bits source out of a public repository and redistribute it.
- Do not include React Bits components in a starter kit, template pack, UI library or npm package that others install.
- Do not sell the components on their own or in a bundle.
- Do not remove the license notice.
- Do not present the components as original work.

## Verify

- The component runs inside the target application.
- The license notice is present.
- Reduced motion stops continuous animation.
- The component works at 320px and 1440px.

## Attribution

React Bits by David Haz, MIT plus the Commons Clause, https://reactbits.dev. Full license: https://github.com/DavidHDev/react-bits/blob/main/LICENSE.md
entries.summary: A large collection of animated React components: text effects, backgrounds, cursor effects, micro-interactions and full components. Installed as source through the shadcn CLI or jsrepo.

entries.title: shadcn/ui
entries.prompt:
# Use shadcn/ui in a project

Source: shadcn/ui, https://ui.shadcn.com, MIT. Pinned upstream commit `96da9cc7f1aa10580a3741664e2a77c721206c00`.
Rights: permissive. Install components as source and keep the MIT notice for substantial portions.

## Goal

Set up shadcn/ui as the primitive layer for a React and Tailwind project, then add only the components the page needs.

## Use it when

- The project is starting and needs accessible primitives with theme tokens.
- The team wants to own and edit component source rather than depend on a runtime library.
- Magic UI or React Bits components will be layered on top.

## Build steps

1. Initialize in a React project with Tailwind and CSS variables:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest init
   ```

2. Add components by name:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add button dialog card input
   ```

3. Review every generated file like your own code. Replace demo copy, narrow props and match the project tokens.
4. Keep the theme tokens in CSS variables. Do not hard-code colors in component files.
5. Add only the primitives the page uses. Add more when a real screen needs them.
6. Keep the MIT notice for substantial portions copied into the project.

## Requirements

- Focus states, labels, disabled states and keyboard behavior are tested, not assumed.
- Dark and light themes both work through tokens.
- The component files are typechecked and linted like application code.
- Imports use the project alias, not deep relative paths across the app.

## Do not

- Do not treat shadcn/ui as a runtime dependency or a package you upgrade blindly.
- Do not copy every component into the project.
- Do not override accessibility behavior without testing it.
- Do not remove the MIT notice for substantial portions.

## Verify

- `npm run build` passes.
- Keyboard navigation works in dialogs, menus and forms.
- The theme switch changes surfaces through tokens.
- No component file contains hard-coded brand colors.

## Attribution

shadcn/ui, MIT, https://ui.shadcn.com. Keep the MIT notice when copying substantial portions.
entries.summary: The base layer for most of the stack indexed here. Components are copied into your project as source, so you own and edit the files. It is not a runtime dependency.

entries.title: Animated Hero
entries.prompt:
# Add Animated Hero to a project

Source: Animated Hero by Tommy Jepsen (https://21st.dev/@tommyjepsen/components/animated-hero), MIT. First published at https://twblocks.com/blocks/heroes/hero5. The published source is `references/animated-hero/AnimatedHero.tsx`.

Rights: permissive. Copy the component, keep the MIT notice and the Tommy Jepsen credit, and state any changes you make.

## Goal

Add a centered hero whose headline swaps one word on a spring, with a launch link and two calls to action under it.

## Use it when

- The page needs a short marketing hero with one moving word, not a full animation system.
- You can supply a list of five to seven short words that fit on one line.
- You have a Button component or can copy the one in `library/button/`.

## Build steps

1. Copy `AnimatedHero.tsx` and `LICENSE.md`.
2. Install the runtime pieces:

   ```bash
   npm install motion lucide-react
   ```

3. Copy `library/button/Button.tsx` and `Button.tsx`'s CSS, or change the `./Button` import to your own button and map `secondary` and `ghost` to your variants.
4. Replace the `titles` array with your words. Keep them short and keep the array stable with `useMemo`.
5. Replace the headline prefix, the paragraph and the three button labels with your copy.
6. Point the buttons at real destinations. Use an anchor for the launch article if it navigates.
7. Confirm `text-foreground` and `text-muted-foreground` exist in your theme, or replace them.
8. Keep the `prefers-reduced-motion` branch. It stops the timer and renders one title in normal flow.
9. Reduce `py-20 lg:py-40` if the hero sits inside a section that already has padding.

## Requirements

- Only one timeout exists at a time, and it is cleared on unmount.
- The active title is the only one exposed to assistive technology.
- The non-breaking space or an equivalent fixed height holds the title line.
- The spring animates transform and opacity only.
- The heading, the paragraph and the buttons remain readable at 390px.
- The buttons are real buttons or links, not divs.

## Do not

- Do not add more than about seven titles. The spring needs time to settle between swaps.
- Do not use long words that pass the width of the heading box. The container clips them.
- Do not remove the placeholder height. The absolute titles will collapse the line.
- Do not run the timer when reduced motion is set.
- Do not keep the upstream `framer-motion` import if your project already ships `motion`. Use one animation library.
- Do not remove the MIT notice or the Tommy Jepsen credit.

## Verify

- The word changes every two seconds and wraps from the last word to the first.
- Unmounting the hero leaves no timer running.
- At 390px the longest word stays inside the heading box.
- With reduced motion, the first word is visible and never swaps.
- Screen readers read one title, not all five.
- Tab reaches the three buttons and the focus ring is visible.
- No layout shift when a longer word replaces a shorter one.

## Attribution

Animated Hero by Tommy Jepsen (https://21st.dev/@tommyjepsen/components/animated-hero), MIT. Copied with the notice kept. Changes are listed in the entry.
entries.summary: A centered marketing hero with one rotating word. "This is something" stays put while amazing, new, wonderful, beautiful and smart swap on a two second timer. Each word enters on a spring, the previous word leaves in the opposite direction, and a row of buttons sits under the copy.

entries.title: Animated Rocket Shader Hero
entries.source_author: Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent) for the shader; component author not recorded
entries.prompt:
# Build a dark shader hero inspired by Animated Rocket Shader Hero

Source: shader derived from Star Nest by Pablo Roman Andrioli, adapted by Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent). The wrapper author is not recorded. License unknown.
Rights: private-reference. **Do not copy the source.** Write an original shader hero.

## Goal

Build a full-screen dark hero with a slow procedural light field behind the copy. The content must remain readable without WebGL2, and the motion must stop for people who ask for less.

## Use it when

- A landing page needs atmosphere without a hero image.
- The product is technical and a calm, dark first screen fits the tone.
- You can afford a WebGL2 canvas and can keep the copy in HTML.

## Build steps

1. Create a React component with one canvas fixed behind absolutely positioned hero content.
2. Write an original fragment shader. A good starting point is layered value noise or fbm with a slow drift and a soft warm core. Do not derive it from Star Nest or any Shadertoy shader.
3. Add a pointer uniform only if the shader actually uses it. Smoothed pointer influence of a few percent is enough.
4. Compile once, cache the program, and resize to the container with the device pixel ratio capped at 2. Do not multiply the ratio twice.
5. Render one static frame when `prefers-reduced-motion` matches. Pause the loop when the canvas is offscreen or the tab is hidden.
6. Put the copy in real HTML: badge, headline, subtitle, one primary and one secondary action. Keep the canvas `aria-hidden`.
7. Stagger the copy reveal at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 seconds with opacity and translate, and remove it under reduced motion.
8. Provide a CSS gradient fallback for browsers without WebGL2.

## Requirements

- Text contrast stays above 4.5:1 against the darkest and brightest part of the canvas.
- No textures, no per-frame allocations and no more than one draw call.
- The shader is disposed and listeners removed on unmount.
- The hero does not block scroll or keyboard navigation.
- A visible focus ring on both actions.

## Do not

- Do not copy the source component, its shader, its markup or its class names.
- Do not use a Star Nest or Shadertoy derivative. Those carry their own licenses and this one is unknown.
- Do not ship a continuous animation without reduced-motion handling.
- Do not use dynamic Tailwind class names that the compiler cannot see.
- Do not put two default exports in one module.
- Do not claim the visual direction as entirely your own. Credit the inspiration.

## Verify

- The hero renders with WebGL2 disabled and the copy is still readable.
- Reduced motion produces a still frame and no entrance animation.
- The page does not scroll horizontally at 320px.
- The render loop stops when the hero scrolls out of view.

## Attribution

Inspired by Animated Rocket Shader Hero, whose shader derives from Star Nest by Pablo Roman Andrioli and the adaptation credited to Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent). License unknown. No source code was copied.
entries.summary: A full-screen dark hero. A WebGL2 fragment shader paints a drifting cloud and light field, and the marketing content sits above it with staggered fade-ins and warm gradient headings.

entries.title: Animated Shiny Text
entries.prompt:
# Add Animated Shiny Text to a project

Source: Animated Shiny Text by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/animated-shiny-text, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Use one line of text with a slow highlight sweep to signal that something is new. The effect should read as an occasional glint, not a loading state.

## Use it when

- A short release note, status line or announcement needs a little life.
- The line is decorative or secondary, not a control label.
- The surface is clearly light or clearly dark, because the gradient uses black and white stops.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/animated-shiny-text`, or copy `AnimatedShinyText.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Render a single `span`. Pass size, weight and color through `className`.
3. Set `shimmerWidth` between 80 and 140 pixels for a short line. Wider values suit longer text.
4. Keep the default keyframes. They rest for most of the cycle, which is what makes the sweep feel occasional.
5. Add the site-level reduced-motion rule that sets `animation: none` on `.animate-shiny-text`.

## Requirements

- The text is readable at the moment the highlight passes underneath it.
- The line does not wrap in the middle of the effect on small screens. Shorten the copy instead.
- The animation is purely decorative. Set `aria-hidden` when the same message already exists in nearby text.

## Do not

- Do not use it for a button label, form label, error message or anything that must be read while moving.
- Do not run several shiny lines at once. One per view is the point.
- Do not rely on the default `max-w-md` or neutral color. Set them for your surface.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- Reduced motion shows static text.
- The sweep does not cause a layout shift.
- The line is legible at 320px and at 1440px.

## Attribution

Animated Shiny Text by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A single line of text with a light highlight that sweeps across it. The effect is a clipped background gradient animated with a CSS keyframe, so no canvas or JavaScript animation loop is involved.

entries.title: Circular Navigation Bar
entries.prompt:
# Build a circular navigation overlay

Build an original circular navigation overlay for a React and Tailwind project. Use this entry as a design brief, not as code: do not copy the Kaif UI source or any file from 21st.dev. The component documented in `references/circular-navigation-bar/entry.md` has no recorded license, so the implementation has to be yours. Credit Kaif UI as the inspiration.

## Use it when

- There are three to eight top-level destinations and a full-screen menu is acceptable.
- The menu is opened deliberately and closed after one choice.
- You can add a focus trap, scroll lock and Escape handling, or the surrounding framework already provides a dialog primitive.

Do not use it for a persistent header with dropdowns, for more than eight destinations, or for a menu that has to sit alongside page content.

## Build steps

1. Make the trigger a real button with `aria-haspopup="dialog"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Keep the label visible.
2. Render the overlay in a portal at the end of `body`. Give it `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"` and an accessible name such as "Main navigation".
3. On open, move focus to the close button. Trap Tab inside the dialog, close on Escape, and return focus to the trigger on close.
4. Lock page scroll while the overlay is open. Use `overflow: hidden` on the root and restore the previous value on close.
5. Size the disc from the viewport with a maximum around 420px. Measure it with `ResizeObserver`.
6. Derive the orbit radius instead of hardcoding it: half the disc minus half a target minus padding. Clamp the target to at least 44px and around 80px when there is room.
7. Place each destination with one angle: `360 / count * index`, starting at the top. Rotate the slot by the angle, translate by the radius, then rotate the content back by the same angle.
8. Fall back to a vertical list when the computed radius is too small, when there is one or two destinations, or when there are more than eight.
9. Give every target a visible `focus-visible` ring, an `aria-current="page"` state for the active destination, and a close button with an accessible name.
10. Animate opacity and a small scale over roughly 250ms. Skip the animation under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.
11. Use `min-height: 100dvh` with a `100vh` fallback, plus safe-area padding.
12. Close on backdrop click, on Escape and on link activation. Stop propagation inside the disc so a click there does not dismiss the menu.

## Requirements

- Keyboard: Tab reaches every destination and the close button; Shift+Tab wraps; Escape closes; focus returns to the trigger.
- Screen readers: the dialog is announced, the trigger reports its expanded state, and the close button has a name.
- Motion: no scale or fade when reduced motion is requested.
- Layout: no target leaves the viewport at 320px, 390px, 768px or 1440px.
- Dependencies: Tailwind plus the project's existing icon set. Do not add `framer-motion` for this alone.

## Do not

- Do not copy the original component, its file names, class strings or markup. Write your own structure.
- Do not hardcode a 150px radius or a fixed 420px disc.
- Do not ship an icon-only close button without a label.
- Do not rely on hover for the only highlight state.
- Do not use `100vh` alone, leave the page scrollable behind the overlay, or omit the focus trap.
- Do not animate when the user prefers reduced motion.

## Verify

- Open with keyboard and pointer, tab through every item, close with Escape, and confirm focus returns to the trigger.
- Test at 320px, 390px, 768px and 1440px with five, seven and nine destinations.
- Check that the disc and every target stay inside the viewport and that the page cannot scroll behind it.
- Turn on reduced motion and confirm the menu appears without a scale transition.

## Attribution

Inspired by Circular Navigation Bar by Kaif UI (https://21st.dev/@kaif-ui/components/cicular-navigation-bar). No license was recorded, so this is an original implementation, not a port. Keep the credit line in the target project.
entries.summary: A full-screen navigation overlay that replaces a list with a circular dial. Up to seven destinations sit evenly around a translucent disc, each one an icon and a label inside a round target. A white circular button in the middle closes the overlay. The disc scales in from nothing while a dimmed backdrop covers the page. Hovering a destination fills it white and flips its icon and text to black.

entries.title: Dot Pattern
entries.prompt:
# Add Dot Pattern to a project

Source: Dot Pattern by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/dot-pattern, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Add a quiet dot grid behind a section without an image request. The pattern should support the content and never compete with it.

## Use it when

- A section needs texture but not a full background illustration.
- A card or stage needs depth behind a headline or a code sample.
- You want a static texture with an optional glow.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/dot-pattern`, or copy `DotPattern.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Place it inside a positioned container with `relative` and `overflow-hidden`. The SVG is absolute and fills the container.
3. Set spacing with `width` and `height` between 16 and 24. Use `cr` around 1 for a fine grid.
4. Color it with a text utility such as `text-stone-900/10` or `text-white/10`.
5. Mask it with `[mask-image:radial-gradient(...)]` so the grid fades instead of ending at a hard edge.
6. Leave `glow` off for reading sections. Turn it on only for a small, focused panel.

## Requirements

- The SVG stays `aria-hidden` and `pointer-events-none`.
- The dot count stays reasonable. Increase spacing or cap the height on very large sections.
- Glow does not run under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Text over the pattern keeps at least 4.5:1 contrast.

## Do not

- Do not put text directly on an unmasked, full-opacity grid.
- Do not use glow behind long paragraphs.
- Do not rely on container resizes. The component listens to window resize only, so remount it or update spacing when a layout change resizes the parent.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The pattern does not intercept clicks or focus.
- The section has no horizontal overflow at 320px.
- Reduced motion removes the glow animation.

## Attribution

Dot Pattern by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A dot grid drawn as SVG circles that fill the parent container. With `glow`, each dot pulses on its own delay. Without it, the pattern is static.

entries.title: Glassmorphism Folder Cards
entries.prompt:
# Add Glassmorphism Folder Cards to a project

Source: Glassmorphism Folder Cards by Kedhareswer Naidu, https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/glass-folder-cards, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy `GlassFolderCards.tsx` from the vault entry or install it from 21st.dev, and you must keep the visible credit and the MIT notice.

## Goal

Place a folder object on the page that behaves like a folder. The front panel is frosted glass over generated artwork and a stack of files. Hovering leans the glass toward the pointer, clicking opens the folder and fans the files out as buttons, and the plus key adds a file.

## Use it when

- The page has a real background or pattern for the glass to blur. On a flat fill the frost is invisible.
- A card can be the main focus of a section, with room above it for the open files.
- The content behind the folder can be generated art or your own image.
- You can test a phone width and a desktop width before shipping.

## Build steps

1. Copy `GlassFolderCards.tsx` into `components/ui/` or install it from its 21st.dev page. It needs React and TypeScript only. Keep the `"use client"` directive if the host uses the Next.js app router.
2. Pass `files` with real names and optional `meta`, `art` or `image`. Without `files` it shows the sample set, which is demo content.
3. Choose `width`. Everything is drawn at 340 by 272 and scaled by `width / 340`, so 260 to 340 is the practical range for a card. Measure the container and cap the width instead of hard-coding 340 in a narrow column.
4. Reserve the root height of 0.96 times the width. The stage leaves 54 units of headroom above the folder for open files, and the visible folder sits below that space.
5. Put a real image or the generated art behind the glass. `art` accepts `aurora`, `ember`, `dusk`, `glacier`, `verdant`, a custom recipe, or `none`; `image` takes your own picture.
6. Wire `onFilesChange` if the added files must survive a reload. `onAdd` only changes the component's internal list.
7. Use `appearDelay` to stagger a row of folders. Set `appear={false}` if the folder starts inside a hidden tab or carousel where it may never intersect the viewport.
8. Add a live region of your own if the file count is important. The roll animation is visual and the component does not announce the new count.

## Requirements

- The folder remains usable by keyboard: Enter or Space opens and closes it, Escape closes it, and the `more` menu supports arrow keys, Home and End.
- Closed files are out of the tab order. The component uses `inert`; keep a modern browser target or add a fallback.
- The label, file names and menu labels remain the accessible text. Do not wrap the whole component in `aria-hidden`.
- The glass has a background to blur and the page still holds 60fps on the phones you support.
- Reduced motion leaves a readable folder even if the entrance and hinge transitions are removed.

## Do not

- Do not remove the author credit or the MIT notice. The license requires the notice, and this vault requires the credit.
- Do not place a modified fork beside the original. Every instance injects the same global `.gf-*` styles, so two versions collide.
- Do not set `files` from a prop you expect to update later. It is read once into state; remount to reset.
- Do not put the folder on a flat background and expect the glass to read. The frost needs something behind it.
- Do not mount many folders with unique recipes and sizes in one viewport. The canvas painter is budgeted but not free.
- Do not assume hover works on touch. Check the tap state and the open state separately.
- Do not present the folder design as your own work.

## Verify

- At the width you ship, the title, count and key do not overlap and the folder silhouette is intact.
- Opening the folder fans the files out, each file is a focusable button, and closing it removes them from the tab order.
- Hovering leans the glass and moves the highlight; opening with the keyboard matches opening with the pointer.
- The plus key drops a file, the count rolls, and `onFilesChange` receives the new list.
- Escape and a click outside close the open folder and the menu.
- On a phone, the folder fits its column with no horizontal scrolling and no clipped fan.
- Reduced motion still shows a legible closed folder and a usable open folder.
- The page has no console errors and the artwork appears after the queue finishes.

## Attribution

Glassmorphism Folder Cards by Kedhareswer Naidu, MIT, published at https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/glass-folder-cards. Keep the credit and the license notice.
entries.summary: A folder you can open, drawn as three real layers instead of a picture of a folder. A back panel holds generated artwork, the files sit between the panels, and a frosted front panel blurs whatever is behind it. Hovering leans the glass toward the pointer, clicking drops the panel and fans the files out as labelled buttons, and the plus key drops a new file into the pocket.

entries.title: Interactive 3D Machine
entries.source_author: Evgeny Shilov (eugeneshilow); built with OpenAI Codex, ported to React by Claude
entries.prompt:
# Build an interactive 3D product machine inspired by Interactive 3D Machine

Source: Interactive 3D Machine by Evgeny Shilov (https://agentic-factory-3d.vercel.app), license unknown.
Rights: private-reference. **Do not copy the source.** Read the public descriptions and write an original scene.

## Goal

Build a React and three.js section where one product is presented as a physical machine with five named stations. The user can orbit the machine, hover and click a station, switch between four levels of detail, and jump between camera presets. The scene must explain the product, not just decorate the page.

## Use it when

- A product has a sequence of five or fewer stages that people keep confusing.
- A static diagram is not enough and a video would be too passive.
- You can afford the three.js bundle and can keep the rest of the page light.

## Build steps

1. Choose the five station names and the one-sentence job of each. Write them down before touching three.js.
2. Scaffold a React component with `react` and `three`. Keep the scene in one module, the controls in another, and the HTML chrome in the component. Do not put the whole thing in one 2,000 line file.
3. Build the machine from primitives: a base plate, five station bodies, connectors, and a few moving parts. Use one environment map for reflections. No downloaded models or images.
4. Add four modes: assembled, cutaway, stations, one order. Each mode changes what is visible and what the camera emphasizes.
5. Add five camera presets: overview, side, top, station and flight. Animate between them with a damped position and target, not a cut.
6. Add raycasting for hover and click. Change the cursor on hover and focus the clicked station. Show the station name in real HTML next to the canvas.
7. Expose a small control object from the component: `setMode`, `setCamera`, `focusStation`, `play`, `pause`. Return it from a ref or an `onReady` callback. Do not attach it to `window`.
8. Add a reduced-motion path that renders a still frame and disables camera flights.
9. Pause rendering when the canvas leaves the viewport or the tab is hidden. Resume on return.

## Requirements

- Canvas has an `aria-label` naming the five stations and the available interactions.
- Every mode and camera control is a real button with `aria-pressed` and a visible focus ring.
- Station names and descriptions exist in HTML, not only in the canvas texture.
- The scene does not trap page scroll. Wheel zoom is disabled unless the user is interacting with the canvas.
- On coarse pointers, allow orbiting or provide explicit rotate buttons. Do not silently disable all rotation.

- Cap the pixel ratio at 2 and keep the machine under roughly 150k triangles.

## Do not

- Do not copy the source, its geometry, its station names or its layout.
- Do not ship a continuously rendering canvas with no visibility check.
- Do not make the canvas the only place where meaning lives.
- Do not use a global `window` object for control.
- Do not claim the original design as yours.

## Verify

- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` shows a still frame and no camera flight.
- Keyboard users can reach every control and read every station name.
- The tab stays near 60fps on a mid-range laptop and does not keep rendering after scrolling away.
- On a phone, the page scrolls normally and the machine remains explorable.

## Attribution

Inspired by Interactive 3D Machine by Evgeny Shilov (https://agentic-factory-3d.vercel.app), license unknown. No source code was copied.
entries.summary: A React and three.js scene of a short-video factory as one physical machine. Five stations sit on a metal plate: engine, admin, storefront, cabinet and cashdesk. entries.title: Interactive Image Accordion
entries.prompt:
# Build an accessible image accordion from scratch

Do not copy the source of Interactive Image Accordion by Le Thanh. The 21st.dev page records `no-license`, so this entry is inspiration only. Write an original component and credit Le Thanh as the inspiration.

## What to build

A row of three to six image panels where one panel is open and the others collapse to labelled spines. Activating a panel expands it, and its caption becomes readable. On small screens the row becomes a vertical stack.

## Requirements

- Render each panel as a real `<button>`, not a `div` with a pointer handler.
- Support click, tap, Enter and Space. Support ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Home and End for moving between panels, with focus following the selection.
- Use a tab pattern or `aria-expanded` with `aria-controls` so assistive technology knows which panel is open, and keep the caption in real text.
- Use one active index in state. Derive sizes from it; do not store five booleans.
- Size panels with flex-grow or grid tracks that fit the container. Never combine fixed 400px and 60px widths with a half-width column.
- Below roughly 700px, switch to a vertical accordion with a fixed open height. Do not leave a horizontally scrolling row on a phone.
- Add a dark gradient behind the caption, not a flat 40% overlay, and check contrast on the brightest image.
- Give images width and height attributes, load the first eagerly and the rest lazily, and supply a local fallback rather than a remote one.
- Use decorative empty alt text when the visible title already names the panel.
- Detect `prefers-reduced-motion` and remove the size transition.
- Do not change the active panel on hover unless the pointer is fine and hovering is a bonus, not the only path.

## Pitfalls

Animating `flex-grow` or `height` still triggers layout. Keep the panel count low, avoid box shadows on the moving edge and test on a mid-range phone. If you animate transforms instead, the images need to be cropped to a fixed frame or they will distort. Keep collapsed titles short; a long word cannot fit a 60px spine even when rotated.

Credit: inspired by Interactive Image Accordion by Le Thanh, published on 21st.dev. No code or images were copied.
entries.summary: A landing section with five tall image panels in a row. The active panel is 400px wide and the rest are 60px spines with rotated titles. Hovering another panel widens it, so the row behaves like an accordion without any vertical collapse.

Liquid Sculpture Hero by Guglielmo Giannattasio, MIT, published at https://21st.dev/@gughigug/components/liquid-sculpture-hero. Keep the credit and the license notice.

entries.prompt:
# Add Marquee to a project

Source: Marquee by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/marquee, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Create a continuous horizontal or vertical strip of cards, labels or logos driven by CSS keyframes, with no JavaScript animation loop.

## Use it when

- A row of principles, logos, testimonials or tags should feel alive.
- The content is decorative or already repeated elsewhere.
- You can keep the motion calm and slow.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/marquee`, or copy `Marquee.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Set `--duration` and `--gap` on the root with arbitrary properties, for example `[--duration:38s] [--gap:1rem]`.
3. Set `repeat` to the number of copies needed to fill the widest viewport. Four is the default.
4. Use `pauseOnHover` for decorative strips, but do not rely on it for keyboard access.
5. Add an edge mask with `[mask-image:linear-gradient(...)]` so items fade rather than cut off.
6. Provide a static, screen-reader-only list of the same content and mark the marquee `aria-hidden`.
7. Keep the Tailwind keyframes for `marquee` and `marquee-vertical` in the theme, and stop them under reduced motion.

## Requirements

- The strip does not cause horizontal page overflow.
- Each item keeps a readable contrast and a consistent width.
- Reduced motion stops the track without hiding the content.
- The strip does not contain a control that keyboard users cannot reach.

## Do not

- Do not put the only copy of meaningful text inside the marquee.
- Do not use hover pause as the only way to stop motion.
- Do not run several marquees in opposite directions in the same view.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The page has no horizontal scrollbar.
- Screen readers read the content once.
- Reduced motion shows the items without movement.

## Attribution

Marquee by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A horizontal or vertical marquee that duplicates its children and scrolls them with CSS keyframes. Duration and gap are CSS variables, and the animation can pause on hover.

entries.title: Mascot Portfolio Hero
entries.prompt:
# Add Mascot Portfolio Hero to a project

Source: Mascot Portfolio Hero by Kedhareswer Naidu, https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/mascot-portfolio-hero, MIT.

Build a portfolio hero where a printed poster layout, a generated one-point room and an illustrated character share one screen. The character follows the pointer with layered parallax, blinks, and greets the visitor when clicked.

## Use it when

- A portfolio or studio page can carry a large illustrated character.
- The page has one screen of copy and does not need a scroll to explain itself.

2. Pass a definite `height` and `minHeight`, for example `height="clamp(560px, 80svh, 780px)"`. Never pass `height="100%"`.

- The hero fits inside its container at both 16:9 and tall portrait shapes.

- Do not remove the author credit or the MIT notice. The license requires the notice, and this vault requires the credit.

- Do not present the component or the character design as your own work.
- Do not add a second copy of the component without checking the duplicated style tag and the global pointer listener.

- At a wide desktop size, the headline, services row, seeking pill and character are all visible and do not overlap.

- Clicking the character changes the greeting and wiggles the beanie tag.

Mascot Portfolio Hero by Kedhareswer Naidu, MIT, published at https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/mascot-portfolio-hero. Keep the credit and the license notice.

A one-point-perspective room is generated in SVG, a four-line display headline fills the left, and an illustrated character stands at the right. The head follows the pointer with layered parallax, blinks on its own, and greets the visitor when clicked.

entries.title: Number Ticker
entries.prompt:
# Add Number Ticker to a project

Source: Number Ticker by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/number-ticker, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Animate a number from a start value to a real target when it scrolls into view, with locale formatting and a spring that settles.

## Use it when

- A stat is already true and worth emphasizing once.
- The number is short enough to read while it animates.
- The section can reserve its final width to avoid layout shift.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/number-ticker`, or copy `NumberTicker.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Pass the real `value`, a sensible `startValue`, and a `delay` between 0 and 0.3 seconds.
3. Use `decimalPlaces` only when the data has decimals. Do not invent precision.
4. Use `direction="down"` when the story is a reduction, such as cost or latency.
5. Reserve width with `tabular-nums` and a `min-width`, so the count does not push the layout.
6. For reduced motion, pass the final value as both `startValue` and `value`. Motion does not detect the preference for you.
7. Keep the label in HTML next to the number, not inside the animated span.

## Requirements

- The number is true at the time of rendering. Do not animate a placeholder.
- The final value is visible without JavaScript.
- The animation runs once when it enters view.
- The label explains the unit and the period.

## Do not

- Do not use it for prices, dates or identifiers.
- Do not stack five tickers in one view.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The final value matches the source data.
- Reduced motion shows the final value immediately.
- No layout shift occurs when the count finishes.

## Attribution

Number Ticker by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A number that springs from a start value to a target when it scrolls into view. Formatting uses `Intl.NumberFormat`, so thousands separators and decimals follow the locale rules of `en-US`.

entries.prompt:
# Add Portal Carousel to a project

Source: Portal Carousel by Hyperiux (https://21st.dev/@hyperiux/components/portal-carousel), Free Core under MPL 2.0. The published source is `references/portal-carousel/PortalCarousel.tsx`.

Rights: permissive. You may copy or install this file, keep the MPL 2.0 notice and the Hyperiux credit, and state any changes you make to it. MPL 2.0 is file-level copyleft: your other files do not become MPL, but this file and its modifications stay MPL.

## Goal

Add a full-stage image carousel where a small preview follows the pointer and expands into the next image on click.

## Build steps

1. Copy `PortalCarousel.tsx` into the project and keep the notice at the top of the file.
2. Install GSAP: `npm install gsap`.
3. Render the component with at least two images:

   ```tsx
   <PortalCarousel
     images={[
       { src: first, alt: "First image", title: "First" },
       { src: second, alt: "Second image", title: "Second" },
     ]}
     label="Next"
   />
   ```

4. Give the stage a height. The component defaults to `h-screen`; inside a card or a section, pass an important height class such as `h-[min(70svh,640px)]!`.
5. Use images with the same aspect ratio. The stage crops with `object-cover`, so mixed ratios will crop differently at each step.
6. If you pass overlay children, remember the wrapper is `pointer-events-none`. Add `pointer-events-auto` to any link or button that must be clickable.
7. Keep the MPL notice and add a visible credit near the component: Portal Carousel by Hyperiux, MPL 2.0.

## Requirements

- At least two images or the control disappears.
- GSAP must be installed. There is no CSS-only fallback for the expansion.
- Alt text is optional but should be supplied for meaningful images; it reaches the live region.
- The preview is a real button. Do not replace it with a div, or keyboard access is lost.
- Reduced motion must stay supported: the source already fades instead of expanding.

## Do not

- Do not hotlink Hyperiux's demo photos from the R2 bucket. They are not covered by the component license.
- Do not remove the license header or the credit.
- Do not put interactive overlay content inside the stage without `pointer-events-auto`.
- Do not rely on the default `h-screen` inside a scrolled page section.
- Do not describe this as an original design. It is Hyperiux's component, hosted under MPL 2.0.

## Verify

- A click anywhere on the stage advances once. Clicking overlay links does not advance.
- Rapid clicks stack expansions without breaking the current index.
- Tab reaches the preview button and Enter advances.
- With reduced motion, the image cross-fades and the preview does not trail.
- On a touch device, the preview parks and tapping the stage advances.
- No layout shift when the images preload, and no horizontal overflow at 320px.

## Attribution

Portal Carousel by Hyperiux (https://21st.dev/@hyperiux/components/portal-carousel), MPL 2.0 (https://mozilla.org/MPL/2.0/). Built with Hyperiux Vault.
entries.summary: A full-stage image carousel where the next image waits as a small square preview near the cursor. A click expands that preview from its parked corner into the whole frame with GSAP, then the following preview appears. Titles and the image count roll over as each image lands.

entries.title: Spotlight Card
entries.prompt:
# Add a pointer-tracked spotlight card to a project

Source: Spotlight Card by Hossain Jahed (https://21st.dev/@jahed/components/spotlight-card). The page records no license.

Rights: private reference. Do not copy the original component, its demo code or its assets. The source is not hosted in this repository. Write an original implementation that credits Hossain Jahed as the inspiration.

## Goal

Build a card whose edge and face catch a soft light that follows the pointer, without a global listener or an injected style block.

## Use it when

- A dark interface needs a tactile hover state on a small set of important cards.
- The cards have room for a border, so the edge glow has something to sit on.
- The design can answer the touch and keyboard cases, not only the mouse.

## Build steps

1. Decide the resting state. A card that is invisible until hovered is a dead card on touch.
2. Add one pointer listener per card, not one on the document. Update two custom properties, such as `--spot-x` and `--spot-y`, in percentage or pixels.
3. Paint a radial gradient at that position on a pseudo-element or an inset overlay. Keep the paint inside the card so nothing leaks.
4. For the border, use a second gradient on a masked ring or a visible border with `border-image` style masking. The surface gradient alone is not an edge light.
5. Add a `focus-visible` state that places the light at a fixed point, so keyboard users see the same affordance.
6. Remove the transition under `prefers-reduced-motion`. Keep the light itself.
7. Reset the position on pointer leave with a short fade, not an instant cut.
8. Expose a small set of tones through a data attribute or a prop, each with its own color token.

## Requirements

- The listener is attached to the card element and removed on unmount.
- The light is made from CSS gradients, not a canvas or an animated image.
- Contrast of the card text must not depend on the glow. Keep body text readable in the resting state.
- Touch and keyboard must have a usable state.
- Scope the CSS to the component. Do not inject a global style tag.

## Do not

- Do not copy the original component, demo markup or glow map. They are unlicensed.
- Do not put a `pointermove` listener on `document` for a grid of cards.
- Do not animate layout properties. Move custom properties or background positions only.
- Do not hide the card content until hover.
- Do not claim the effect as an original idea. Credit Hossain Jahed.

## Verify

- The glow follows the pointer on the border and the face, at 1440px and at 390px.
- Tab focus shows the light without a pointer.
- Touch shows a stable resting card.
- Reduced motion removes the transition, not the highlight.
- No global style tag and no document-level pointer listener.
- Text contrast passes in both the resting and the lit state.

## Attribution

Inspired by Spotlight Card by Hossain Jahed (https://21st.dev/@jahed/components/spotlight-card). No code or assets copied. This repository's implementation is original and MIT licensed.
entries.summary: A card whose border and surface light up under the pointer. A soft radial glow follows the cursor across the edge, while the card face picks up a weaker tint in the same place. Several named glow colors and sizes are offered.

entries.title: Zoom Parallax
entries.prompt:
# Build a zoom parallax scene from scratch

Do not copy the source of Zoom Parallax by Efferd. The 21st.dev page records no license for that component, so this entry is inspiration only. Write an original scene and credit Efferd in a comment or credits line.

## What to build

A sticky full-viewport stage with five to seven image panels. One scroll progress value drives a different scale ceiling for each panel, between roughly 3x and 8x, so the collage appears to move through depth. The stage should hold for at least two viewport heights, then release into the next section.

## Requirements

- Use one scroll listener or one `useScroll` target for the whole scene. Do not attach a listener per panel.
- Keep the stage inside a section that is tall enough to scroll, and make sure no ancestor uses overflow clipping.
- Size the panels in percentages of the stage, not in viewport units alone. Write a small-screen composition that hides two or three panels instead of shrinking all seven into slivers.
- Supply images at least twice the rendered panel size, or reveal them with `clip-path` rather than upscaling raster pixels.
- Add width and height attributes, decode asynchronously, and load the first two panels eagerly and the rest lazily.
- Detect `prefers-reduced-motion` and render a static collage without transforms. Do not leave a tall empty scroll region in that mode.
- Use empty alt text on the panels if the scene is decorative, and mark the stage `aria-hidden`. Keep any real copy in HTML outside the stage.
- Use `svh` or `dvh` for the sticky stage height so mobile browser chrome does not cover it.
- If you add smooth scrolling, stop its animation frame and destroy the instance on unmount.

## Pitfalls

A single scroll progress value works only while the section is on screen. If an anchor link lands in the middle of the section, the progress starts partly through the zoom. Decide whether that is acceptable or reset the progress on entry. Avoid Lenis and similar libraries unless the page already uses them; they can fight the browser's native scrolling and accessibility.

Credit: inspired by Zoom Parallax by Efferd, published on 21st.dev. No code or images were copied.
entries.summary: A scroll scene made of seven images on one sticky stage. The stage holds for three viewport heights while each image scales at a different rate, from 4x to 9x, so the composition appears to pull apart and push through the screen.

entries.prompt:
# Add the UI Vault Button to a project

   ```tsx
   <Button variant="danger" disabled>Delete</Button>
   ```

   ```css
     --ui-button-bg: #0f766e;
     --ui-button-hover: #115e59;
     --ui-button-focus: #0f766e;
   ```

Source: Interactive Robot Card by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT, `library/interactive-robot-card/`.

Add a dark card with copy on one side and an original three.js robot on the other. The robot turns toward the pointer, without a model file, a skeleton or three.js in the first bundle.

## Use it when

- A dark section needs one 3D character next to a headline.
- You want pointer-aware motion without animation clips or a Spline dependency.
- The card can carry the message in text, because the canvas is decorative.

## Build steps

1. Copy `InteractiveRobotCard.tsx` and `interactive-robot-card.css`.
2. Install three.js:

   ```bash
   npm install three
   npm install -D @types/three
   ```

3. Import the component and pass a height:

   ```tsx
   <InteractiveRobotCard height="clamp(460px, 66vh, 620px)" headingLevel="h2" />
   ```

4. Put the card on a dark background, or let the card provide its own. The component sets `#0b0b09` and the copy colours.
5. Replace the title, body and the three chips in `robot-card__meta`.
6. Keep the dynamic `import("three")` inside the effect. A top-level import puts the whole library in the entry bundle.
7. Keep the pointer listener on the card. Do not move it to `document`.
8. Keep the cleanup block. It disposes the geometries, the materials, the observers and the WebGL context.

## Requirements

- The canvas stays `aria-hidden` and the copy stays outside it.
- The canvas keeps `pointer-events: none`; the card is the pointer target.
- The head yaw and pitch stay within the pointer range, and the lenses move inside the visor.
- `prefers-reduced-motion` renders one frame, resets the pose and stops the loop.
- The loop pauses offscreen and when the tab is hidden.
- WebGL failure shows a readable status line and the copy stays readable.
- Touch does not get gaze tracking, and vertical scrolling still works.
- The card has a height on desktop and a minimum height when it stacks on mobile.

## Do not

- Do not import three.js at the top of the file.
- Do not mount several cards on one page. One scene per page is the budget.
- Do not put essential text inside the canvas or remove the copy.
- Do not attach the pointer listener to `document`, and do not keep it after unmount.
- Do not swap the lens material for a standard one without an emissive colour; the eyes will go dark.
- Do not widen the pointer mapping without clamping the head angles.
- Do not present the robot as the Spline demo character. It is an original three.js model. Keep the Serafim credit as inspiration.

## Verify

- The card renders at 1440px and 390px with no horizontal overflow.
- Moving the pointer turns the head and shifts both lenses, and leaving the card returns the robot to rest.
- Scrolling the card out of view stops the animation loop.
- Reduced motion shows a still robot and the pointer has no effect.
- Blocking WebGL shows the fallback line and the copy stays readable.
- The three.js chunk loads only when the card mounts.
- Keyboard focus never lands on the canvas.

## Attribution

Interactive Robot Card by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT. Inspired by Spline Scene by Serafim (https://21st.dev/@serafimcloud/components/splite). No Spline runtime, component code, scene asset or character model was used.
entries.summary: A dark card with a headline on the left and a robot on the right. The robot is a metallic head with a glossy visor, two lit lenses, ear discs, an antenna and a floating shell, hovering over two thin rings. Source: Spotlight Glow Card by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT, `library/spotlight-glow-card/`.

Add a dark card whose border and face catch a pointer-tracked light, with a keyboard focus state and a usable resting state on touch.

## Use it when

- The interface is dark or has a dark section where a warm light reads well.
- The cards are important enough to deserve a hover detail, but not so many that a pointer listener per card is a cost.
- You can support a focus state for keyboard users.

1. Copy `SpotlightGlowCard.tsx` and `spotlight-glow-card.css`.

   ```tsx
   <SpotlightGlowCard
     eyebrow="01 / Pointer"
     title="Follow the light"
     description="The edge catches the pointer first, then the face."
     tone="amber"
     meta="CSS only"
   />
   ```

- The border and face light follow the pointer at 1440px and 390px.
- Tab shows the outline and the light on every card.
- A touch emulation shows the resting light.
